extraction.name: BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions
extraction.description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions, where each example consists of a question, a Wikipedia passage containing the answer, and a yes/no label. The dataset is designed to test models' ability to perform complex, non-factoid inference and entailment-like reasoning.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified (e.g., starting with indicator words like 'did', 'do', 'does'). Questions were kept if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five results. Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) determining if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, factual), (2) finding a passage within the document containing the answer, and (3) marking the answer as 'yes' or 'no'. The dataset combines 13k questions from this pipeline with 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia passages
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were filtered to focus on yes/no questions. Annotators selected passages containing the answer and marked questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information. The dataset includes only questions marked as having a yes/no answer, paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document to reduce ambiguity.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) determining if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, factual), (2) finding a passage within the document containing the answer, and (3) marking the answer as 'yes' or 'no'. Annotators could mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information. Three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality, achieving 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was assessed by three authors on 110 randomly selected examples, achieving 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels. Of the disagreements, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Due to high agreement, singly-annotated examples were used in the training/dev/test sets to gather a larger dataset.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset contains a class imbalance with 62.31% 'yes' answers in the train set. Questions were categorized into topics and types, with correlations between question nature and likelihood of a 'yes' answer, though these correlations were too weak to outperform the majority baseline.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset may not generalize well to all types of yes/no questions due to its focus on naturally occurring questions from specific sources (Google search queries and Wikipedia). The class imbalance (62.31% 'yes' answers) may bias models. The dataset is limited to questions that can be answered with a yes/no label based on a single Wikipedia passage, which may not capture all real-world complexities.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation for natural language understanding tasks, particularly reading comprehension and entailment-like inference. The dataset is intended for research on transfer learning and model evaluation in question answering tasks.
